n: Jesus wants His people to give to the poor, but warns against giving to be seen. Seeking human praise forfeits the Father’s reward.

f.g: Gifts to help the poor.

n: Don’t blow a trumpet when you give, as hypocrites do in public places to win admiration. The applause they get is their only reward.

f.g: From Greek for “stage actor”: someone performing a role.
They are paid in full already; nothing more is coming.

n: Give so quietly that even your left hand doesn’t know what your right is doing, a vivid picture of not keeping score.
Give in secret, and your Father, who sees what is hidden, will reward you openly.

f.w: thy Father who seeth in secret

n: Don’t pray like hypocrites who stand in public places to be seen praying.

f.g: Busy intersections where many would notice.

n: Instead, go into a private room, shut the door, and pray to your Father in secret. He will reward you openly.

f.g: A private inner room.

n: Don’t use empty, mechanical repetitions like those who think more words get more attention.

f.g: Empty, thoughtless phrases repeated without meaning.
Those who did not know the true God.

n: Your Father already knows what you need before you ask. Prayer is about relationship, not informing God.
The Lord’s Prayer begins: “Our Father who art in heaven,” and His name is to be treated as holy. This is a pattern, “after this manner,” not a script.

f.g: Honored as holy.

n: May God’s will be done on earth as in heaven. Notably, this version omits “Thy kingdom come,” perhaps because the King Himself is present with them.

f.g: Matthew 6:10 also has “Thy kingdom come”; it is absent here.

n: Forgive us our debts as we forgive others. This version also leaves out the request for daily bread; some suggest it is because the Twelve are about to be told the Father will provide.

f.g: A Jewish way of speaking of sins as debts owed to God.
Matthew 6:11 “Give us this day our daily bread” is not in this version.

n: Don’t lead us into temptation, but rescue us from evil. The Joseph Smith Translation reads “suffer us not to be led into temptation.”
The prayer closes by giving God the kingdom, power, and glory forever. Amen.

f.g: Hebrew for “so be it” or “truly.”

n: Jesus explains one line: if you forgive others, the Father forgives you.

f.g: Wrongs; offenses.

n: If you won’t forgive, your Father won’t forgive you. Forgiving others is part of receiving forgiveness.
When fasting, don’t look gloomy and messy to show off your devotion, like hypocrites do. That attention is their only reward.

f.g: Face; expression.
Make unsightly; here, deliberately looking unkempt.

n: Instead, groom yourself normally, oil your hair and wash your face, so no one can tell.

f.g: Put oil on the hair, part of ordinary daily grooming then.

n: Fast for the Father, who sees in secret, and He will reward you openly.
Don’t store up treasures on earth, where moths, rust, and thieves can destroy or take them.

f.g: Moths ruined fine clothing, a common form of wealth then.

n: Store up treasures in heaven, which nothing can ruin or steal.
Your heart follows your treasure. What you value most shapes who you become.
The eye is the body’s lamp. If your eye is “single,” focused wholly on God, your whole self fills with light.

f.g: Undivided; focused on one purpose.

n: If your eye is evil, greedy or divided, your whole self is darkened. When the light within is actually darkness, the darkness is profound.

f.g: In Hebrew idiom, an “evil eye” often means stinginess or greed.

n: No one can serve two masters. You cannot serve God and Mammon, wealth treated as a god.

f.g: An Aramaic word for wealth or riches, pictured here as a rival master.

n: Jesus turns to His twelve chosen disciples. As full-time ministers, they should not worry about food, drink, or clothing. In the Book of Mormon, this counsel is directed specifically to the Twelve.

f.g: Matthew 6:25 addresses a general audience; here Jesus speaks to His ministers.
Don’t be anxious or preoccupied.

n: Look at the birds. They don’t plant, harvest, or store in barns, yet the Father feeds them. Aren’t you worth much more?
Can worrying add a single cubit, about a foot and a half, to your height? Anxiety changes nothing.

f.g: About 18 inches; the length of a forearm.
Height, or possibly length of life.

n: Why worry about clothing? Consider the wildflowers: they don’t work or spin thread.
Yet even King Solomon in all his splendor wasn’t dressed as beautifully as one of them.
If God clothes wild grass that is burned for fuel the next day, He will surely clothe you, unless your faith is small.
So don’t fret over what to eat, drink, or wear.

f.g: With what; by what means.

n: Your Father in heaven knows you need these things.
Put God’s kingdom and righteousness first, and everything else will be given to you as well. Priorities matter.

f.w: seek ye first the kingdom of God

n: Don’t worry about tomorrow; tomorrow will take care of itself. Each day has enough trouble of its own.

f.w: Sufficient is the day unto the evil thereof
f.g: Each day has enough difficulty of its own; don’t borrow tomorrow’s.
